thread.title_full: Nearly 70 percent of Medicare Advantage plan leaders expect leaner benefits in 2027, with Part B givebacks and dental among the cuts - NewsBreak

author: Tyler Foster
title: Nearly 70 percent of Medicare Advantage plan leaders expect leaner benefits in 2027, with Part B givebacks and dental among the cuts - NewsBreak
text:
By Tyler Foster ,
1 days ago
HealthScape Advisors, a health care consultancy owned by the Chartis Group, surveyed more than 35 Medicare Advantage plan executives in January 2026 and found that nearly 70 percent expect their 2027 benefit packages to be less generous than this year’s, a sharp reversal from a year earlier when only 10 percent of the same audience predicted a decline and none forecast richer coverage this time. Axios reported afterward that plan leaders are specifically weighing smaller or eliminated Part B premium givebacks, thinner dental allowances and higher specialist copays as concrete 2027 changes. The shift traces to a federal payment increase insurers describe as too small to keep pace with medical costs.
HealthScape Advisors’ outlook survey marks a reversal from a year of optimism The consultancy behind the survey fields it annually, drawing responses from more than 35 plan executives spanning national insurers, Blues affiliates and provider-sponsored plans, gathered in January 2026 before most insurers had locked their 2027 bids. The comparison to the prior year captures the swing most starkly: not one respondent forecast richer benefits for 2027, compared with 10 percent who expected an improvement in the survey covering 2026. Nearly 70 percent this year said their overall benefit package would be less rich, a figure the consultancy frames as evidence that the industry has moved from incremental trims toward a broader pullback in what a plan promises members.
HealthScape Advisors’ own write-up of the survey points first to supplemental extras such as transportation benefits, over-the-counter allowances and meal deliveries as the categories most likely to shrink, while noting that core supplemental benefits like dental, vision and hearing coverage are expected to remain standard offerings even as their generosity narrows. That distinction matters, because Axios reported that plan leaders are weighing smaller or eliminated Part B premium givebacks, reduced dental allowances and higher specialist copays as concrete changes for next year, a sharper list than the survey’s own broader language about supplemental extras.
The gap the survey leaves: HealthScape’s finding that nearly 70 percent of plan executives expect leaner 2027 packages says nothing about which plan, in which county, is cutting Part B givebacks or dental allowances, a comparison every enrollee still has to run individually once each plan’s own notice arrives, using The 2027 Medicare Open Enrollment Decision Kit .
A federal payment rate insurers call too thin to cover this year’s costs CMS’s final CY2027 rate announcement , issued April 6, 2026, set a net average payment increase of 2.48 percent, worth more than $13 billion in additional Medicare Advantage payments industry-wide next year. Insurers have said in earnings calls that an increase near that size does not keep pace with rising medical and prescription costs, a gap HealthScape’s survey results suggest plans are closing by trimming benefits rather than raising the premiums CMS still has to approve.
The 2.48 percent figure represents a sharp deceleration from the year before. CMS’s own CY2026 rate announcement , issued in April 2025, had set a 5.06 percent increase worth more than $25 billion, roughly double both the percentage and the dollar figure insurers are working with for 2027. That year-over-year drop in the size of the federal raise lines up closely with the timing of HealthScape’s survey and the specific benefit categories plan leaders named.
Humana, the second-largest Medicare Advantage insurer, has told investors it is targeting a sustainable pre-tax margin of at least 3 percent by 2028, a target it has pursued partly by paring back some of the same supplemental categories HealthScape’s respondents flagged. That target illustrates the arithmetic behind the broader trend: a payment increase insurers call inadequate, paired with margin goals insurers have already stated publicly, leaves benefit design as one of the few levers a plan controls without raising a premium CMS has to sign off on first.
What a Part B giveback cut and a narrower dental allowance change on a bill A Part B premium giveback lets a Medicare Advantage plan use part of its rebate dollars to cover some or all of a member’s Part B premium, a benefit that shows up directly in the monthly Social Security deduction rather than in a plan’s marketing brochure. Shrinking or eliminating that giveback for 2027 would raise what a member effectively pays each month even if the plan’s own premium stays listed at zero, the opposite of what a “zero-premium” plan description implies to someone comparing options.
Dental coverage ranks among the most heavily used Medicare Advantage supplemental benefits, and HealthScape’s survey lists it among the areas insurers are narrowing rather than dropping outright, through smaller annual allowances or tighter provider networks rather than removing the benefit from a plan’s materials. Specialist copays, the third category Axios named, would raise a fixed per-visit cost for cardiologists, oncologists and other specialists that plans currently price lower to attract members managing chronic conditions.
A member who compares a 2026 Evidence of Coverage against a 2027 Annual Notice of Change line by line would see any Part B giveback change stated as a dollar amount subtracted from the standard Part B premium, while a dental change typically appears as a lower annual maximum allowance rather than a removed category, and a specialist copay change appears as a revised dollar figure next to each specialist visit type. Reading those three line items together, rather than relying on a plan’s overall star rating or marketing summary, is what turns HealthScape’s industry-wide forecast into a decision specific to one household’s own plan.
None of those specific 2027 benefit summaries were final when HealthScape fielded its survey, since CMS does not require plans to file their Annual Notice of Change until closer to Open Enrollment, which runs October 15 through December 7 . Until those notices reach members, the nearly 70 percent figure works as an early signal from the executives setting next year’s benefits rather than a confirmed count of which plans and counties will see reductions.
